titre: A Statement on Race, Demolished Within a Year
accroche: In 1950, a UNESCO committee wrote that race is “less a biological fact than a social myth.” A year later, a second committee withdrew the phrase.
contenu_vulgarise:
In December 1949, UNESCO brought together eight researchers in Paris: sociologists, anthropologists, a geneticist. Among them, the anthropologist Ashley Montagu was appointed rapporteur; he is the one who drafted the final text. Published and reported in the press as early as July 18, 1950, it stated that mental capacities are similar across human groups, that no evidence shows biological degeneration from the mixing of populations, and that no correlation exists between a nation or a religion and any given race. Its most discussed sentence goes further: race is presented there as “less a biological fact than a social myth,” with biology instead supporting, according to the text, a “universal brotherhood” among men.

## A Statement Other Scholars Judge Indefensible

The text aimed at a clear goal: to answer scientifically, five years after the fall of the Nazi regime, the racial theories that had served to justify extermination. But the “social myth” phrase triggered pushback from a camp one might expect to side with its defenders: geneticists and physical anthropologists, among them the statistician Ronald Fisher, the hereditarian Cyril Darlington, and the geneticist Reginald Ruggles Gates, judged that the 1950 committee claimed more than science actually established. Denying that populations can be distinguished on biological grounds was not, to them, correcting one error, it was committing another.

UNESCO then reassembled a second committee, this time dominated by geneticists, with Leslie Clarence Dunn as rapporteur. Before publishing, the organization sent the draft to ninety-six scientists for comment. The text that emerged, in June 1951, was markedly more cautious: it withdrew the claim that biology would prove universal brotherhood, and acknowledged that populations could be classified by inherited racial traits, while repeating that no hierarchy of value follows from this.

## Two Statements, Not One

The episode is often told as though science had, once and for all, delivered its verdict on race in 1950. The reality is more awkward for anyone looking for a single authority: the more assertive version was judged indefensible by other scientists within a year, and the one that succeeded it had to retreat on its strongest point to win the agreement of a far wider circle of specialists. This proves neither that the first was right and the second wrong, nor the reverse. It proves that the line between a biological fact and a social category was never settled by a single stroke, even one signed by eight experts seated in the same room and reported the same day in the world press. It was negotiated, through successive committees, between disciplines that do not measure scientific caution the same way.

repere.texte: Before publishing its 1951 version, UNESCO sent the second committee's draft to ninety-six scientists for comment.

carte.punch: A UNESCO statement on race, judged indefensible by other scholars within a year.
carte.idee: In July 1950, a UNESCO committee wrote that race is a social myth rather than a biological fact. Geneticists challenged the phrase; a second committee, dominated by geneticists, published a more cautious version in 1951 that withdrew that point.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Montagu's role as rapporteur of the 1950 committee, and the career of the anthropologist who drafted the text.

quiz.question: Why does UNESCO publish a second statement on race as early as 1951, a year after the first?
choix: Because the French government refuses to distribute the 1950 text in its schools
Because geneticists judge that the 1950 phrase about a “social myth” goes beyond what science establishes
Because Ashley Montagu resigns from the committee before the work is finished
Because the United Nations demands a shorter version of the original text
quiz.explication: The 1950 text claimed that race was less a biological fact than a social myth; geneticists such as Fisher and Darlington judged the claim scientifically untenable, leading to a more cautious version in 1951, written by a committee with a majority of geneticists.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who drafts the final text of the 1950 statement, as the committee's rapporteur?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Ashley Montagu, the only physical anthropologist on the 1949 committee, is appointed its rapporteur and drafts the text published in July 1950. Dunn will be the rapporteur of the second committee, in 1951; Lévi-Strauss sat on the first committee without being its rapporteur.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the 1951 statement withdraw compared with the 1950 one?
choix: Any mention of Ashley Montagu's work
The entire 1950 text, replaced wholesale with nothing in common
The claim that biology would prove a “universal brotherhood” among men
The publication date, pushed back a year
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1951 version drops the claim that biology would support universal brotherhood, while keeping the essential point: no hierarchy of value between human groups.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What step does UNESCO take before publishing the 1951 version that the 1950 committee had not taken?
choix: It holds a public vote in member states
It sends the draft to ninety-six scientists for comment
It has the text translated into a hundred languages before publication
It asks for the approval of the United States government
quiz_supplementaire.explication: After the backlash triggered by the 1950 text, UNESCO widens its consultation by sending the 1951 draft to ninety-six scientists, to secure broader agreement before publication.
